column2: From ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not part of it — it is rejected.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. In a narration of Muslim: “Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair — it is rejected.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, from his paternal aunt ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her). Its wordings differ, but their meanings are close; one of them is: “Whoever introduces into our religion something that is not in it — it is rejected.”

This hadith is one of the great foundations of Islam. It is like a scale for deeds in their outward form, just as the hadith “Deeds are only by intentions” is a scale for deeds in their inward reality. Just as every deed done without seeking the Face of Allah the Exalted

brings its doer no reward, so every deed that is not in accordance with the command of Allah and His Messenger is rejected and thrown back on its doer; and whatever anyone introduces into the religion that Allah and His Messenger have not permitted has no part in the religion at all.
The hadith of al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah will come later, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever of you lives on after me will see much disagreement.

So hold fast to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me; bite on to it with your molar teeth. And beware of newly introduced matters, for every newly introduced matter is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance.”
In his sermons he ﷺ used to say: “The truest speech is the Book of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muḥammad,

and the worst of matters are those newly introduced.” We shall leave the discussion of newly introduced matters until we reach the hadith of al-ʿIrbāḍ just mentioned. Here we shall speak about deeds that are not in accordance with the command of the Lawgiver, and their rejection.

By its explicit wording, then, this hadith shows that every deed not in accordance with the Lawgiver's command is rejected; and by its implied meaning it shows that every deed in accordance with that command

is not rejected. What is meant by his “command” (amr) here is his religion and his law, just as that is what is meant by his words in the other narration: “Whoever introduces into this affair (amr) of ours something that is not part of it — it is rejected.”
The meaning, then, is that whoever acts outside the Sharīʿah, unbound by it, has his deed rejected.

His words “not in accordance with our affair” indicate that the deeds of everyone who acts ought to fall under the rulings of the Sharīʿah, with those rulings governing them through their commands and prohibitions.
So when someone's deeds run under the rulings of the Sharīʿah and conform to them, they are accepted; and when they fall outside them, they are rejected.
Deeds are of two kinds: acts of worship and transactions.
As for acts of worship, any of them that lies wholly outside the ruling of Allah and His Messenger is rejected and thrown back on the one who does it, and he falls under His words:

“Or do they have partners who have laid down for them as religion what Allah has not permitted?” [al-Shūrā 42:21]. So whoever seeks to draw near to Allah by a deed that Allah and His Messenger have not made a means of drawing near to Him

has a deed that is void and rejected. His case resembles that of the people whose prayer at the House was whistling and clapping [al-Anfāl 8:35]. Examples are seeking to draw near to Allah the Exalted by listening to musical instruments,
or by dancing, or by baring the head outside the state of iḥrām, and similar innovations through which Allah and His Messenger never prescribed seeking nearness at all.
Nor is what is an act of nearness in one form of worship an act of nearness everywhere else without qualification. The Prophet ﷺ saw a man standing in the sun and asked about him, and was told

that he had vowed to stand and not sit, not to take shade, and to fast. The Prophet ﷺ ordered him to sit and take shade, and to complete his fast. He did not treat his standing and his exposure to the sun as acts of nearness that his vow obliged him to fulfil.
It is narrated that this took place on a Friday, as the man listened to the sermon of the Prophet ﷺ while he was on the pulpit,
and that he had vowed to stand and not sit or take shade for as long as the Prophet ﷺ was preaching, out of reverence for hearing the sermon of the Prophet ﷺ.

Yet the Prophet ﷺ did not treat this as an act of nearness that his vow obliged him to fulfil, even though standing is an act of worship in other settings — in prayer, in the call to prayer and in supplication at ʿArafah — and exposure to the sun is an act of nearness for someone in iḥrām.

This shows that not everything that is an act of nearness in one setting is an act of nearness in every setting; in this one follows only what the Sharīʿah has laid down, in the places where it has laid it down.
The same applies to someone who seeks nearness through an act of worship that has been specifically forbidden, such as fasting on the day of ʿĪd or praying at a time when prayer is forbidden.
As for someone who performs a deed that is prescribed in principle and is an act of nearness, but then introduces into it something not prescribed, or leaves out of it something prescribed,
he too has contravened the Sharīʿah, to the extent of what he left out or introduced. Is his deed then rejected from the root, or not?

No unqualified answer of rejection or acceptance can be given here; instead one must look closer. If what he left out — one of the deed's parts or conditions — is something whose omission makes it void under the Sharīʿah,
as when someone leaves out purification for the prayer though he is able to perform it, or leaves out bowing, or prostration, or stillness in them,
then his deed is rejected, and he must repeat it if it was obligatory. If what he left out does not make the deed void,

as when someone leaves out praying the obligatory prayer in congregation — according to those who hold congregation obligatory without making it a condition [of the prayer's validity] — then it is not said that his deed is rejected from the root; it is merely deficient.

If he has added to the prescribed deed something not prescribed, his addition is rejected, in the sense that it is not an act of nearness and earns no reward. Sometimes, however, it makes the deed void from the root,

so that the deed is rejected — as when someone deliberately adds a rakʿah to his prayer, for example — and sometimes it neither voids the deed nor rejects it from the root, as when someone performs wuḍūʾ washing each part four times, or fasts the night along with the day

and joins fast to fast without a break. Sometimes, again, part of what is commanded in an act of worship is replaced with something forbidden, as when someone covers his nakedness in prayer with a forbidden garment, or performs wuḍūʾ for the prayer with usurped water,
or prays on usurped ground. Scholars have disagreed over this: is his deed rejected from the root, or is it not rejected, so that it discharges his obligation?
Most jurists hold that it is not rejected from the root. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī reported of a group of the theologians of kalām called
the Shimriyyah, followers of Abū Shimr, that they hold that whoever prays in a garment one dirham of whose price was unlawful must repeat his prayer. He said:

“I have never heard a viler view than theirs; we ask Allah for wellbeing.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī was one of the greatest jurists among the hadith scholars and well acquainted with the positions of the Salaf,
and he denounced this view and counted it an innovation. This shows that no one among the Salaf was known to hold that the prayer must be repeated in a case like this.

Similar to this is performing Ḥajj with unlawful wealth. A hadith has come saying that such a Ḥajj is rejected and thrown back on the one who made it, but it is not an established hadith. Scholars have disagreed over whether the obligation is discharged by it or not.

Close to this is slaughtering with a forbidden instrument, or slaughter by someone not entitled to slaughter, such as a thief. Most scholars said that the animal slaughtered in this way is lawful, while some said it is unlawful. There is the same disagreement over game slaughtered by someone in iḥrām, but there the view that it is unlawful is better known and more evident,
because that act is forbidden in itself.

For this reason some scholars distinguished between a prohibition made for a reason specific to the act of worship, which voids it, and one not specific to it, which does not. Praying with impure matter on one, or without purification, or without covering, or facing away from the qiblah voids the prayer,

because the prohibition is specific to prayer — unlike praying on usurped property. This is supported by the fact that a fast is voided only by committing what is forbidden in it specifically, namely eating, drinking and intercourse and what falls under them, and not by what the fasting person is forbidden for reasons not specific to fasting, such as lying and backbiting, according to the majority.
Likewise Ḥajj is voided only by what is forbidden specifically in iḥrām, namely intercourse; it is not voided by forbidden acts not specific to iḥrām, such as killing, theft and drinking wine.

Likewise iʿtikāf is voided only by what is forbidden in it specifically, namely intercourse. In our school and that of most scholars it is voided by intoxication only because the intoxicated person is forbidden to approach or enter the mosque, on one of the two interpretations of His words, the Exalted, “Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated” [al-Nisāʾ 4:43]: that what is meant is the places of prayer.

So he became like a menstruating woman. In our school and that of many scholars, iʿtikāf is not voided by any other major sin the person commits, though a group of the Salaf disagreed, among them ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī, al-Thawrī and Mālik, and this has been reported from others as well.

As for transactions — contracts, their annulment and the like — any of them that alters the arrangements laid down by the Sharīʿah, such as turning the prescribed punishment for fornication into a financial penalty, and the like, is rejected from the root, and ownership does not pass by it,
because such a thing is unknown among the rulings of Islam. This is shown by what the Prophet ﷺ said to the man who asked him: “My son was a hired labourer for so-and-so,

and he committed fornication with his wife, so I ransomed him with a hundred sheep and a servant.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “The hundred sheep and the servant are to be returned to you, and your son is to receive a hundred lashes and a year's banishment.”

Then there are contracts that the Sharīʿah forbids — whether because the thing contracted over is not a valid subject for the contract, or because one of its conditions is missing, or because of a wrong it does to the other party or to what is contracted over,

or because the contract distracts from the obligatory remembrance of Allah when its time is running short, or for some other reason. Is such a contract rejected entirely, so that ownership does not pass by it, or not?
People have been greatly confused on this point, because in some cases it is reported that such a contract is rejected and confers no ownership, and in others that it does; hence the confusion.

The view closest to the truth, if Allah the Exalted wills, is this. If it was forbidden on account of a right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it confers no ownership at all — by a right of Allah we mean one that is not waived by the consent of the contracting parties.

If it was forbidden on account of the right of a particular human being, such that it is waived by his consent, then it depends on his consent: if he consents, the contract is binding and ownership stands; if he does not, he may annul it.

If the person harmed is someone whose consent is not taken into account at all, like the wife in divorce and the slave in manumission, neither his consent nor his displeasure counts. And if the prohibition was purely out of kindness to the one prohibited, because of the hardship it would cause him, and he disobeyed and took the hardship upon himself, his deed is not made void by that.
The first kind has many forms.

One is marrying a woman whom it is unlawful to marry, whether because of who she is — like the women permanently unlawful through affinity or lineage — or because of combining [two who may not be married together], or because a condition is missing that cannot be waived by mutual consent: such as marrying a woman in her waiting period or in iḥrām,

or marrying without a guardian, and the like. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ separated a man from a woman he had married while she was pregnant, and rejected the marriage because it had taken place during her waiting period.
Another is usurious contracts: they confer no ownership, and the parties are ordered to reverse them. The Prophet ﷺ ordered a man who had sold one ṣāʿ of dates for two ṣāʿs to reverse the sale.
Another is the sale of wine, carrion, pigs, idols and dogs, and everything else whose sale is forbidden and which may not be sold even by mutual consent.
The second kind has a number of forms.

One is a guardian marrying off, without her permission, a woman whom he may marry off only with her permission. The Prophet ﷺ rejected the marriage of a previously married woman whose father had married her off against her will,

and it is narrated from him that he gave a choice to a woman who had been married off without her permission. Whether such a marriage is void, or depends on ratification, is the subject of two reported positions from Aḥmad.

A group of scholars held that when someone disposes of another person's property without his permission, the disposal is not void from the root but depends on the owner's ratification: if he ratifies it, it stands, and if he rejects it, it is void.
They took as evidence the hadith of ʿUrwah ibn al-Jaʿd, who bought two sheep for the Prophet ﷺ when he had told him to buy only one, and then sold one of them; and the Prophet ﷺ accepted that.
In the well-known position reported from him, Imam Aḥmad restricted this to someone who disposes of another's property with permission and then goes beyond what was permitted.
Another is a sick person [in his final illness] disposing of all his property: is the disposal void from the root, or does his disposal of the two-thirds depend on the heirs' ratification?

There is a well-known disagreement on this among the jurists, and within the school of Aḥmad and others. It is authentically reported that the case was brought to the Prophet ﷺ of a man who freed six slaves of his at his death

when he had no other property. He summoned them, divided them into three parts, freed two and kept four in slavery, and spoke harshly of the man. Perhaps the heirs had not ratified the freeing of them all; and Allah knows best.

Another is a sale involving concealment of defects and the like — such as the sale of a muṣarrāh [an animal left unmilked to make its udder look full], najsh [bidding up the price with no intention of buying], going out to meet caravans [to buy from them before they reach the market], and so on. The validity of all of these is the subject of well-known disagreement within the school of Imam Aḥmad, and a group of hadith scholars held them void and rejected.

The correct view is that such a sale is valid and depends on the ratification of whoever was wronged by it. It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he gave the buyer of a muṣarrāh the option [to return it],

and gave the caravan riders the option once they had come down to the market. All of this shows that such sales are not rejected from the root. The hadith of the muṣarrāh was put to one of those who held such sales void, and no answer from him is recorded.

As for a town-dweller selling on behalf of a desert-dweller: those who held it valid placed it in this category, while those who held it void regarded the right involved as belonging to all the people of the town. They are too many to count, so waiving their rights is inconceivable, and it becomes like a right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Another: if someone sells slaves whom it is unlawful to separate — a mother and her child, say — and separates them, is the sale void and rejected, or does it depend on their consent?
It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ ordered such a sale to be reversed, and Aḥmad stated explicitly that it is not permissible to separate them even if they consent.

A group held that separating them with their consent is permissible, among them al-Nakhaʿī and ʿUbaydullāh ibn al-Ḥasan al-ʿAnbarī. On that view, it would follow that the sale is valid but depends on their consent.

Another: if someone singles out some of his children for a gift and not others. It is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that when Bashīr ibn Saʿd singled out his son al-Nuʿmān for a gift, he ordered him to take it back.
That does not show that ownership did not pass to the child, for such a gift is valid but takes effect provisionally.
If he then makes his children equal in giving, or takes back what he gave the child, that is permissible. If he dies without doing either, Mujāhid said

that it becomes part of the estate; something similar is reported from Aḥmad, namely that the gift becomes void. The majority hold that it does not become void. Do the heirs then have the right to take it back or not?
There are two well-known views on this, which are two reported positions of Aḥmad.
Another is a forbidden divorce, such as divorce during menstruation. It has been said that this was forbidden for the husband's sake, since it was feared that he might come to regret it,

and whoever is forbidden something out of kindness to him, but does not refrain and goes ahead and bears the hardship, is not judged to have done something void — like someone who fasts while ill or travelling,
or joins fast to fast, or gives away all his wealth and then sits begging from people, or prays standing though standing harms him because of illness, or bathes though he fears harm to himself

or death, and does not perform tayammum, or fasts every day without breaking his fast, or stands the whole night in prayer without sleeping. The same applies to pronouncing three divorces together, on the view that this is unlawful.

It has also been said that divorcing a menstruating woman was forbidden only for the woman's sake, because it harms her by lengthening her waiting period. If she consents to it — by asking him for a divorce in return for compensation during her period — is the prohibition then lifted?

There are two well-known views among the scholars; the well-known position of our school and of al-Shāfiʿī's is that it is lifted. If it is said that the prohibition exists solely for the husband's sake, then when he goes ahead with the divorce he has waived his right, and so it lapses. And if the reason given is that it exists for the woman's sake,

that too does not prevent the divorce from being effective and taking place, for the woman's consent is not a condition for a divorce to take effect, according to all Muslims; no one disagrees on this except a tiny band of the Rāfiḍah and their like. In the same way a slave's consent to his manumission is not taken into account,

even if it harms him. But if the woman is harmed by it, and some of her divorces remain, the husband is ordered to take her back, just as the Prophet ﷺ ordered Ibn ʿUmar to take back his wife, to remedy the harm to her

and to remedy the forbidden divorce he had pronounced, so that her final separation from him would not arise from a forbidden divorce, and so that he could divorce her in a permissible way and her separation would come about in that manner.

It is narrated from Abū al-Zubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ returned her to him and did not consider it anything. Of all Ibn ʿUmar's students, Abū al-Zubayr alone narrated this; the others include
his son Sālim, his freedman Nāfiʿ, Anas, Ibn Sīrīn, Ṭāwūs, Yūnus ibn Jubayr, ʿAbdullāh ibn Dīnār, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Maymūn ibn Mihrān and others.

The leading scholars, hadith scholars and jurists alike, rejected this wording from Abū al-Zubayr. They said he was alone in narrating something that contradicts the reliable narrators, so what he alone narrates is not accepted;
for the narration of the many from Ibn ʿUmar shows in many ways that the Prophet ﷺ counted the divorce against him.

Ibn ʿUmar used to say to anyone who asked him about divorce during menstruation: “If you pronounced one divorce or two, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered me to do this” — meaning to take the woman back — “but if you pronounced three, you have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife is separated from you.”

Abū al-Zubayr's narration has a further addition in which no one corroborates him, namely his words: Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: “O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period, and keep count of the waiting period” [al-Ṭalāq 65:1]. None of the narrators from Ibn ʿUmar mentioned this.
Rather, ʿAbdullāh ibn Dīnār narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he himself used to recite this verse when narrating the hadith, and this is what is correct.
Various people believed that Ibn ʿUmar's divorce had been a triple divorce, and that the Prophet ﷺ returned her to him only

because divorce does not take effect during menstruation. This too has been narrated from Abū al-Zubayr, in the narration of Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār al-Duhnī from him. So perhaps Abū al-Zubayr believed this to be true

and narrated that wording according to the meaning he understood. Ibn Lahīʿah narrated this hadith from Abū al-Zubayr, saying “from Jābir”: that Ibn ʿUmar divorced his wife while she was menstruating, and the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Let him take her back, for she is his wife.” He erred in mentioning Jābir in this chain, and he alone narrated the words “for she is his wife” — words that would imply the divorce had not taken effect only if it were assumed to have been a triple one.

So the narrations of this hadith from Abū al-Zubayr conflict, whereas there is no conflict among Ibn ʿUmar's reliable students, the ḥāfiẓ narrators who knew him well and kept close to him. Ayyūb narrated

from Ibn Sīrīn, who said: For twenty years I was told by people I did not suspect that Ibn ʿUmar divorced his wife three times while she was menstruating, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to take her back.

I would not suspect them, yet I could not make sense of the hadith, until I met Abū Ghallāb Yūnus ibn Jubayr, who was a man of sound reliability. He told me that he had asked Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿUmar told him that he had divorced her once. Muslim recorded it.
In one narration Ibn Sīrīn said: I could see no way to make sense of the hadith, and could not understand it.
This shows that it had spread among reliable narrators who were not people of jurisprudence and knowledge that Ibn ʿUmar's divorce had been a triple divorce,
and perhaps Abū al-Zubayr was one of these. That is why Nāfiʿ was often asked about Ibn ʿUmar's divorce: was it triple or single?

When Nāfiʿ came to Makkah, people sent to him from the circle of ʿAṭāʾ to ask him about it, because of this confusion. Ibn Sīrīn's disbelief at the report of a triple divorce shows that he knew of no one of any standing who held that a forbidden divorce does not take effect, and that such a view has no basis.
Imam Aḥmad, in the narration of Abū al-Ḥārith, was asked about someone who said that a forbidden divorce does not take effect
because it contradicts what was commanded. He said: “This is a bad, worthless view,” and then mentioned the story of Ibn ʿUmar and how he counted the divorce he had pronounced during menstruation.

Abū ʿUbayd said: “That it takes effect is what the scholars agree upon in every region — the Ḥijāz and Tihāmah, Yemen and al-Shām, Iraq and Egypt.” Ibn al-Mundhir reported the same from every person of knowledge whose view is preserved, apart from some people of innovation who are not taken into account.

As for Ibn Ḥazm's report from Ibn ʿUmar that divorce during menstruation does not take effect, he relied on what he narrated by way of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Salām al-Khushanī al-Andalusī: Muḥammad ibn Bashshār told us,

ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Thaqafī told us, from ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, concerning a man who divorces his wife while she is menstruating: he said, “It is not counted”; and with his chain something similar from Khilās.

But a word has dropped from the end of this report: he said, “That menstrual period is not counted.” That is how Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah narrated it in his book from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Thaqafī, and so too Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn narrated it

from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, saying: “It is unusual (gharīb); only ʿAbd al-Wahhāb narrated it.” What Ibn ʿUmar meant is that the woman does not count the menstrual period in which she was divorced as one of the periods (qurūʾ) of her waiting term, and this is what Khilās and others meant too.
The same has also been narrated from a number of the Salaf, among them Zayd ibn Thābit and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib,

and a number of Qurʾān commentators and others made a mistake, as Ibn Ḥazm did, and reported from some of those we have named that divorce during menstruation does not take effect. This is the cause of their mistake; and Allah knows best.

Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad narrated this hadith when he was asked about a man who had three dwellings and bequeathed a third of the three: should the bequest be gathered together for the beneficiary in a single dwelling?

He said: “All of it is to be gathered into one dwelling. ʿĀʾishah told me that the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair — it is rejected.’” Muslim recorded it.

He meant that changing a testator's bequest to what is more beloved to Allah and more beneficial is permissible. This view is reported from ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Jurayj, and some of those who hold it may cite His words, the Exalted:

“But whoever fears from a testator some deviation or sin, and makes peace between them, there is no sin upon him” [al-Baqarah 2:182]. Perhaps al-Qāsim took this from the way the freeing of slaves was gathered together,
for it is authentically reported “that a man freed six slaves at his death, and the Prophet ﷺ summoned them, divided them into three parts, freed two and kept four in slavery.” Muslim recorded it.
The jurists among the hadith scholars followed this hadith,

because completing a slave's freedom wherever possible is better than freeing him in part. That is why the extension of freedom to the rest of the slave (sirāyah) and the slave's earning the value of the remainder (siʿāyah) were prescribed when one of two partners frees his share of a slave.
And he ﷺ said of someone who freed part of a slave of his: “He is entirely free; Allah has no partner.”
Most scholars disagree with al-Qāsim's view here: a testator's bequest is not gathered together; his wording is followed, except in manumission specifically,
because the reason for gathering it together in manumission does not exist in other kinds of property, so in them the bequest is carried out as the testator specified.
A group of jurists held, concerning manumission, that a third of each slave is freed and the slaves are made to work to earn the rest;
but following the judgement of the Prophet ﷺ is more fitting and more deserving. Al-Qāsim considered that the beneficiary's sharing with the heirs in all the dwellings would harm them,

so this harm was to be lifted from them by gathering the bequest into one dwelling; for Allah has made it a condition of bequests that they cause no harm, in His words, the Exalted: “without causing harm — an ordinance from Allah” [al-Nisāʾ 4:12]. Whoever causes harm by his bequest has his deed rejected, because he has contravened the condition Allah laid down for bequests.

A group of jurists held that if someone bequeathed a third of all his dwellings, and then two-thirds of the dwellings were destroyed and a third remained, the whole of what remains is given to the beneficiary. This is the view of a group of Abū Ḥanīfah's followers,

and it is reported from Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad [al-Shaybānī]; al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā of our school agreed with them in his al-Khilāf. They based this on the view that jointly owned dwellings may be divided among the co-owners by compulsory division, which is the view of Mālik

and the apparent meaning of what Ibn Abī Mūsā of our school says. The well-known position in our school is that several separate dwellings are not subject to compulsory division, which is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī.

Some Mālikīs interpreted al-Qāsim's fatwa mentioned in this hadith as referring to a case where one of the two parties — the heirs or the beneficiaries — asked for the dwellings to be divided, and they were close enough together to be combined with one another in the division;
in that case, on their view, the request for division would be granted. But this interpretation is far-fetched and goes against the apparent meaning; and Allah knows best.
